claim: Synaptotagmin 7 and Doc2 have both been proposed as Ca2+ sensors that trigger asynchronous neurotransmitter release.
source: Synaptotagmin (syt) 7 and Doc2 have both been proposed as Ca2+ sensors that trigger this mode of exocytosis, but conflicting findings have led to controversy.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established scientific debate in the field.

claim: At excitatory mouse hippocampal synapses, Doc2α is the major Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous release.
source: Here, we demonstrate that at excitatory mouse hippocampal synapses, Doc2α is the major Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous release, while syt7 supports this process through activity-dependent docking of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by multiple experimental approaches including iGluSnFR imaging, electrophysiology, and electron microscopy.

claim: Syt7 supports asynchronous release through activity-dependent docking of synaptic vesicles.
source: Here, we demonstrate that at excitatory mouse hippocampal synapses, Doc2α is the major Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous release, while syt7 supports this process through activity-dependent docking of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electron microscopy data showing syt7's role in vesicle docking dynamics.

claim: In synapses lacking Doc2α, asynchronous release after single action potentials is strongly reduced.
source: In synapses lacking Doc2α, asynchronous release after single action potentials is strongly reduced, while deleting syt7 has no effect.
evidence: This finding is supported by iGluSnFR imaging and electrophysiology data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Deleting syt7 has no effect on asynchronous release after single action potentials.
source: In synapses lacking Doc2α, asynchronous release after single action potentials is strongly reduced, while deleting syt7 has no effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated by iGluSnFR imaging and electrophysiology experiments in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In the absence of syt7, docked vesicles cannot be replenished on millisecond timescales.
source: However, in the absence of syt7, docked vesicles cannot be replenished on millisecond timescales.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data showing failure of vesicle docking recovery in syt7 KO neurons.

claim: Both synchronous and asynchronous release depress from the second pulse onward during repetitive activity in syt7 knockout synapses.
source: Consequently, both synchronous and asynchronous release depress from the second pulse onward during repetitive activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by train stimulation experiments using iGluSnFR imaging and electrophysiology in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Synapses lacking Doc2α have normal activity-dependent docking.
source: By contrast, synapses lacking Doc2α have normal activity-dependent docking, but continue to exhibit decreased asynchronous release after multiple stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 6 showing normal docking dynamics in Doc2α KO neurons.

claim: Synapses lacking Doc2α continue to exhibit decreased asynchronous release after multiple stimuli.
source: By contrast, synapses lacking Doc2α have normal activity-dependent docking, but continue to exhibit decreased asynchronous release after multiple stimuli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by train stimulation experiments in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Disruption of both Doc2α and syt7 is non-additive with respect to asynchronous release.
source: Moreover, disruption of both Ca2+ sensors is non-additive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by epistasis experiments using double knockout mice in Figure 8.

claim: Syt7 drives activity-dependent docking, providing synaptic vesicles for synchronous (syt1) and asynchronous (Doc2 and other unidentified sensors) release during ongoing transmission.
source: These findings result in a new model whereby syt7 drives activity-dependent docking, thus providing synaptic vesicles for synchronous (syt1) and asynchronous (Doc2 and other unidentified sensors) release during ongoing transmission.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by integration of all experimental data and mathematical modeling.

claim: Synchronous neurotransmitter release sets in after tens of microseconds of a stimulus and completes within several milliseconds.
source: Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release involves at least two kinetically distinct components: one is synchronous, and sets in after tens of microseconds (Sabatini and Regehr, 1996) of a stimulus and completes within several milliseconds.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Asynchronous neurotransmitter release sets in more slowly and can persist for tens or hundreds of milliseconds.
source: The other component is asynchronous; it sets in more slowly and can persist for tens or hundreds of milliseconds (Goda and Stevens, 1994; Kaeser and Regehr, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Synaptotagmin isoforms 1 and 2 are the Ca2+ sensors for synchronous release.
source: The molecular basis of synchronous release has been characterized in depth, and there is broad agreement that the underlying Ca2+ sensors are two members of the synaptotagmin (syt) family of proteins, isoforms 1 and 2 (Stevens and Sullivan, 2003).
evidence: This is established scientific consensus, supported by citation.

claim: The Ca2+ sensors that regulate asynchronous release remain a subject of controversy.
source: The Ca2+ sensors that regulate asynchronous release (AR), however, remain a subject of controversy.
evidence: This statement characterizes the state of the field and is supported by the conflicting literature discussed.

claim: Asynchronous release is thought to play a critical role in information processing and circuit function.
source: AR is thought to play a critical role in information processing and circuit function (Iremonger and Bains, 2007; Kaeser and Regehr, 2014; Manseau et al., 2010) and has been implicated in epileptiform activity in rats and humans (Jiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Asynchronous release has been implicated in epileptiform activity in rats and humans.
source: AR is thought to play a critical role in information processing and circuit function (Iremonger and Bains, 2007; Kaeser and Regehr, 2014; Manseau et al., 2010) and has been implicated in epileptiform activity in rats and humans (Jiang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Doc2α mediates asynchronous release in hippocampal neurons.
source: Two isoforms of Doc2, α and β, function as Ca2+ sensors; α mediates AR in hippocampal neurons, and loss of AR in α knockout (KO) neurons can be rescued by β (Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of asynchronous release in Doc2α knockout neurons can be rescued by Doc2β.
source: Two isoforms of Doc2, α and β, function as Ca2+ sensors; α mediates AR in hippocampal neurons, and loss of AR in α knockout (KO) neurons can be rescued by β (Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both Doc2 and syt7 exhibit slow Ca2+-regulated membrane-binding kinetics and high affinity required for asynchronous release.
source: Both Doc2 and syt7 exhibit the slow Ca2+-regulated membrane-binding kinetics and high affinity required for AR (Hui et al., 2005; Xue et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Doc2α drives significant levels of asynchronous release both after single action potentials and during trains in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: In cultured hippocampal neurons, we previously found that Doc2α drives significant levels of AR both after single action potentials and during trains (Gaffaney et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2018; Xue et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Doc2α's activity in asynchronous release depends on Ca2+ binding.
source: This activity depends on Ca2+ binding (Xue et al., 2018; Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: No significant changes in asynchronous release were observed in Purkinje cell to deep cerebellar nuclei synapses lacking Doc2.
source: However, no significant changes in AR were observed in Purkinje cell to deep cerebellar nuclei synapses (Khan and Regehr, 2020) and in autaptic cultured hippocampal neurons lacking Doc2 (Groffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature showing conflicting results.

claim: No significant changes in asynchronous release were observed in autaptic cultured hippocampal neurons lacking Doc2.
source: However, no significant changes in AR were observed in Purkinje cell to deep cerebellar nuclei synapses (Khan and Regehr, 2020) and in autaptic cultured hippocampal neurons lacking Doc2 (Groffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature showing conflicting results.

claim: Syt7 is important for asynchronous release during sustained activity at the zebrafish neuromuscular junction.
source: Syt7 is important for AR during sustained activity at the zebrafish neuromuscular junction (Wen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No synaptic phenotypes were initially observed in syt7 KO mouse cortical neurons.
source: In syt7 KO mouse cortical neurons, no synaptic phenotypes were initially observed (Maximov et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Defects in asynchronous release were found when deleting syt7 or preventing it from binding Ca2+ in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Later studies found defects in AR when deleting syt7 or preventing it from binding Ca2+ in cultured hippocampal neurons (Bacaj et al., 2013), in the cerebellum at inhibitory synapses formed between basket cells and Purkinje neurons as well as at granule cell synapses (Chen et al., 2017; Turecek and Regehr, 2018), and at excitatory synapses between pyramidal cells and Martinotti neurons in the neocortex (Deng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deleting syt7 decreased asynchronous release after a single action potential only in granule cell synapses and in syt1 KO cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Among these studies, deleting syt7 decreased AR – after a single action potential – only in granule cell synapses (Turecek and Regehr, 2018) and in syt1 KO cultured hippocampal neurons (Bacaj et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In inhibitory synapses of the inferior olive, deleting syt7 makes release slower.
source: In inhibitory synapses of the inferior olive, where release after single action potentials is often highly asynchronous, deleting syt7 actually makes release even slower (Turecek and Regehr, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In WT neurons, 64% of release events occurred at the first 10 ms time point (synchronous release) after a single stimulus.
source: In WT neurons, 64% of release events occurred at the first 10 ms time point (synchronous release: n = 1000 release events); the rest of the events (36%) were defined as asynchronous (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments presented in Figure 1C.

claim: EGTA-AM treatment greatly reduced asynchronous release in WT neurons (88% synchronous and 12% asynchronous).
source: This treatment greatly reduced AR (Figure 1C; 88% synchronous and 12% asynchronous).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments with EGTA-AM treatment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Syt7 KO neurons had 66% synchronous and 34% asynchronous release after a single stimulus.
source: Syt7 KO neurons had no apparent phenotype (Figure 1C and D; 66% synchronous and 34% asynchronous; p=0.39, Dunnett's test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments presented in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Doc2α KO neurons had 84% synchronous and 16% asynchronous release after a single stimulus.
source: By contrast, the asynchronous component was markedly reduced in Doc2α KO neurons (Figure 1B and C; 84% synchronous and 16% asynchronous).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Peak average fluorescence intensity in both Doc2α and syt7 mutants was similar to WT.
source: The peak average fluorescence intensity in both mutants was similar to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that synchronous release is not affected in these mutants (Vevea et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In acute hippocampal slices, syt7 KOs showed no phenotype in EPSC amplitude and kinetics after a single stimulus.
source: As with iGluSnFR imaging in cultured neurons (Figure 1), syt7 KOs showed no phenotype – the amplitude and kinetics of EPSCs were nearly identical to those of WT (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: In Doc2α KO acute slices, the EPSC amplitude was unchanged after a single stimulus.
source: By contrast, in Doc2α KO, the EPSC amplitude was unchanged, but the total charge transfer was reduced by 35% (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: In Doc2α KO acute slices, the total charge transfer was reduced by 35% after a single stimulus.
source: By contrast, in Doc2α KO, the EPSC amplitude was unchanged, but the total charge transfer was reduced by 35% (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The slow, asynchronous component of EPSCs decreased by 61% in Doc2α KO neurons after a single stimulus.
source: However, the slow, asynchronous component decreased by 61% in Doc2α KO neurons (p<0.0001, Dunnett's test) and 10% in syt7 KO neurons (Figure 2D; p=0.15), though this latter difference was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices presented in Figure 2D.

claim: EGTA-AM treatment of WT slices reduced the slow component of EPSCs by 74%.
source: EGTA-AM treatment of WT slices reduced the slow component by 74% (Figure 2B–D; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices presented in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The time constants for both components of evoked EPSCs were similar across all genotypes after a single stimulus.
source: Finally, the time constants for both components of evoked EPSCs were similar across all genotypes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices presented in Figure 2D.

claim: WT neurons exhibited slight facilitation of synchronous release in response to the second pulse during train stimulation.
source: At both 10 and 20 Hz, WT neurons exhibited slight facilitation of synchronous release (measured as the peak average fluorescence intensity) in response to the second pulse, and thereafter depressed as the train went on, eventually reaching a steady state (Figure 3B and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments during train stimulation presented in Figure 3B and D.

claim: The asynchronous fraction gradually increased during the train at both 10 and 20 Hz stimulation frequencies in WT neurons.
source: In addition, the asynchronous fraction gradually increased during the train at both stimulation frequencies (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments during train stimulation presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation was similar between WT and Doc2α KO neurons.
source: We examined the first two responses in the train and found that paired-pulse facilitation was similar between WT and Doc2α KO neurons (WT: 1.04 ± 0.06, Doc2α KO: 1.03 ± 0.04, p=0.9953, with an interstimulus interval (∆t) = 100 ms; WT: 1.31 ± 0.08, Doc2α KO: 1.28 ± 0.08, p>0.9191, ∆t = 50 ms, Dunnett's test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Doc2α KO neurons, synaptic depression set in more slowly from the third action potential onward during train stimulation.
source: However, in KO neurons, synaptic depression set in more slowly from the third action potential onward, eventually reaching the same steady-state depression as WT later in the train.
evidence: This is a finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments during train stimulation.

claim: Syt7 KO neurons displayed paired-pulse depression instead of facilitation.
source: In contrast, syt7 KO neurons displayed paired-pulse depression instead of facilitation (syt7 KO: 0.57 ± 0.03, p<0.0001, Δt = 1001 ms; syt7 KO: 0.52 ± 0.03, p<0.0001, Δt = 50 ms, Dunnett's test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as well as faster and more severe synaptic depression as the train progressed (Figure 3D), consistent with previous reports (Chen et al., 2017; Jackman et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2014; Vevea et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3D.

claim: Asynchronous release was decreased in Doc2α KOs, but not syt7 KOs, in response to the first pulse in the stimulus train.
source: As in the single-stimulus measurements (Figure 1), AR was decreased in Doc2α KOs, but not syt7 KOs, in response to the first pulse in the stimulus train.
evidence: This is a finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments during train stimulation.

claim: From the second action potential onward during train stimulation, both Doc2α and syt7 KOs yielded reductions in asynchronous release compared to WT.
source: However, from the second action potential onward, both KOs yielded reductions in AR compared to WT, such that by the end of the train the fraction of AR was reduced by 53 and 50% in syt7 and Doc2α KO neurons, respectively (Figure 3A–C; see also Vevea et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from iGluSnFR imaging experiments during train stimulation presented in Figure 3A-C.

claim: No spatial segregation of asynchronous release was observed during the first two responses in train stimulation.
source: To test such a possibility, we analyzed the distribution of the iGluSnFR signals from 923 boutons. We did not observe spatial segregation of AR during the first two responses (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for further analysis and details).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of iGluSnFR imaging data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: During 20 Hz stimulation in hippocampal slices, peak amplitudes depressed more slowly in Doc2α KO compared to WT.
source: Namely, during 20 Hz stimulation, peak amplitudes (synchronous release) depressed more slowly in Doc2α KO, and syt7 KO neurons had faster and more profound synaptic depression during the train, compared to WT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices during train stimulation presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Syt7 KO neurons had faster and more profound synaptic depression during 20 Hz train stimulation compared to WT.
source: Namely, during 20 Hz stimulation, peak amplitudes (synchronous release) depressed more slowly in Doc2α KO, and syt7 KO neurons had faster and more profound synaptic depression during the train, compared to WT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices during train stimulation presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of syt7 caused more severe synaptic depression than EGTA-AM during train stimulation.
source: Interestingly, loss of syt7 caused more severe synaptic depression than EGTA-AM.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices during train stimulation.

claim: Syt7 and Doc2α KO neurons both exhibited 65% reductions in the tonic charge transfer component during train stimulation.
source: This approach revealed that syt7 and Doc2α KO neurons both exhibited 65% reductions in the tonic charge transfer component, while EGTA-AM treatment reduced tonic charge by 74% (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices during train stimulation presented in Figure 4C.

claim: EGTA-AM treatment reduced tonic charge by 74% during train stimulation.
source: This approach revealed that syt7 and Doc2α KO neurons both exhibited 65% reductions in the tonic charge transfer component, while EGTA-AM treatment reduced tonic charge by 74% (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electrophysiology experiments in acute slices during train stimulation presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Unstimulated syt7 and Doc2α KO synapses appeared qualitatively normal by electron microscopy.
source: Unstimulated syt7 and Doc2α KO synapses appeared qualitatively normal (see Figures 5A–D and 6A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for example micrographs).
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy experiments presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Knocking out either Doc2α or syt7 did not affect the number of docked vesicles at rest.
source: Knocking out either protein did not affect the number of docked vesicles at rest (Figure 6D and E) nor the number and distribution of synaptic vesicles within 100 nm of the plasma membrane at the active zone (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electron microscopy experiments presented in Figure 6D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In syt7 KOs, the number of exocytic pits at each time point after stimulation was not different from the corresponding WT control.
source: In syt7 KOs, this sequence was unchanged: the number of pits at each time point in the KO was not different from the corresponding WT control (pits per synaptic profile: syt7 KO: no stim: 0.04 pits; 5 ms: 0.28 pits; 11 ms: 0.14 pits; 14 ms: 0.06 pits; p>0.9 for each compared to the corresponding syt7 WT time point, Brown–Forsythe ANOVA with Games–Howell post hoc test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electron microscopy experiments measuring exocytic pits.

claim: In Doc2α KO synapses, the number of exocytic pits at 5 ms was unchanged, but pits at 11 ms were almost completely abolished.
source: By contrast, in Doc2α KO synapses, the number of pits at 5 ms was unchanged, but pits at 11 ms were almost completely abolished (pits per synaptic profile: Doc2α KO: no stim: 0.02 pits; 5 ms: 0.32 pits; 11 ms: 0.03 pits; 14 ms: 0.01 pits; p=0.04 between WT and KO 11 ms, p=0.02 between WT no stim and 11 ms, p>0.9 between KO no stim and 11 ms, Brown–Forsythe ANOVA with Games–Howell post hoc test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electron microscopy experiments measuring exocytic pits.

claim: Doc2α accounts for 54–67% of asynchronous release at hippocampal excitatory synapses after a single action potential.
source: In sum, we obtained the same result from three different techniques (iGluSnFR imaging, patch-clamp electrophysiology, and zap-and-freeze electron microscopy): after a single action potential, Doc2α accounts for 54–67% of AR at hippocampal excitatory synapses, whereas deleting syt7 has no effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integration of multiple experimental approaches.

claim: WT controls showed rapid depletion and replenishment of docked vesicles after an action potential.
source: WT controls showed rapid depletion and replenishment of docked vesicles after an action potential, as previously reported (Kusick et al., 2020; Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy experiments presented in Figure 6E and F, consistent with prior work.

claim: At 5 and 11 ms after stimulation, there were ~40% fewer docked vesicles than in the no stimulation controls in WT neurons.
source: At 5 and 11 ms, there were ~40% fewer docked vesicles than in the no stimulation controls, then at 14 ms docked vesicles returned to baseline (Figure 6E and F; docked vesicles per synaptic profile: syt7 WT: no stim: 2.19; 5 ms; 1.52; 11 ms: 1.36; 14 ms: 1.93; Doc2α WT: no stim: 1.90; 5 ms: 0.91; 11 ms: 1.00; 14 ms: 1.62; see Figure 5—figure supplement 2A for active zone sizes from each condition and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C for docked vesicle data normalized to the size of active zones, and Figure 5—source data 2 for full descriptive statistics and test statistics).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electron microscopy experiments presented in Figure 6E and F.

claim: In syt7 KO neurons, there were ~25% fewer docked vesicles than in WT controls at 5 ms and 11 ms after stimulation.
source: In syt7 KO neurons, consistent with our previous data (Vevea et al., 2021), there were ~25% fewer docked vesicles than in WT controls at 5 ms and 11 ms.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electron microscopy experiments, consistent with prior work.

claim: At 14 ms after stimulation, docked vesicles completely failed to recover in syt7 KO, remaining at less than half of the no-stim control.
source: At 14 ms, docked vesicles completely failed to recover in syt7 KO, remaining at less than half of the no-stim control (docked vesicles per synaptic profile: syt7 KO: no stim: 2.12; 5 ms: 1.07; 11 ms: 1.07; 14 ms: 1.09; p<0.0001 between WT and KO at 14 ms, p=0.001 at 5 ms between WT and KO, p=0.16 at 5 ms between WT and KO, Brown–Forsythe ANOVA with Games–Howell post hoc test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: Syt7 is absolutely required for transient docking of synaptic vesicles.
source: These data indicate that syt7 is absolutely required for transient docking of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from electron microscopy data showing failure of docking recovery in syt7 KO.

claim: In Doc2α KO neurons, normal docked vesicle depletion and faster recovery were observed.
source: In Doc2α KO neurons, by contrast, we observed normal docked vesicle depletion and faster recovery (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy experiments presented in Figure 6F.

claim: The number of docked vesicles was 40% greater in Doc2α KO than in WT at 11 ms after stimulation.
source: The number of docked vesicles was 40% greater in the KO than in the WT at 11 ms, about halfway toward full recovery to baseline (docked vesicles per synaptic profile: Doc2α KO: no stim: 1.85; 5 ms; 1.11; 11 ms: 1.40; 14 ms: 1.63; p<0.0001 between WT and KO at 11 ms, p<0.0001 between 11 ms and no stim in the KO, Brown–Forsythe ANOVA with Games–Howell post hoc test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: Transient docking completely fails in the absence of syt7.
source: We conclude that transient docking completely fails in the absence of syt7, while Doc2α is dispensable for docked vesicle recovery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from electron microscopy data.

claim: Doc2α is dispensable for docked vesicle recovery.
source: We conclude that transient docking completely fails in the absence of syt7, while Doc2α is dispensable for docked vesicle recovery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from electron microscopy data.

claim: Syt7 supports synchronous and asynchronous release after multiple stimuli by triggering transient docking.
source: Taken together with our data on exocytosis, these results suggest that syt7 supports synchronous and asynchronous release after multiple stimuli by triggering transient docking, while Doc2α is a Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous fusion itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integration of electron microscopy and functional data.

claim: Doc2α is a Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous fusion itself.
source: Taken together with our data on exocytosis, these results suggest that syt7 supports synchronous and asynchronous release after multiple stimuli by triggering transient docking, while Doc2α is a Ca2+ sensor for asynchronous fusion itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integration of electron microscopy and functional data.

claim: The mathematical model assumes docking of synaptic vesicles occurs in two steps: first tethering, then docking to become fusion competent.
source: As in previously proposed models (Miki et al., 2016; Neher and Brose, 2018; Pan and Zucker, 2009; Walter et al., 2013; Weingarten et al., 2022), we assumed docking of synaptic vesicles to occur in two steps: first, synaptic vesicles are tethered to release sites before they dock and become fusion competent (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model structure, based on prior modeling approaches.

claim: In the model, vesicle exocytosis depends on the total number of Ca2+ ions bound to syt1 and Doc2α per vesicle/release site.
source: Vesicle exocytosis in the model depends on the total number of Ca2+ ions bound to syt1 and Doc2α per vesicle/release site, and is simulated using an adaptation of previously developed dual-sensor models (Kobbersmed et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model structure.

claim: In the model, each Ca2+ ion bound to either syt1 or Doc2α lowers the energy barrier for vesicle fusion.
source: In this model, each Ca2+ ion bound to either sensor was assumed to lower the energy barrier for vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model structure.

claim: In the model, the rate of fusion increases exponentially as more Ca2+ ions are bound to syt1 and Doc2α.
source: This means that the rate of fusion increases exponentially as more Ca2+ ions are bound to syt1 and Doc2α (Schotten et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model structure, supported by citation.

claim: In the model, the fusion rate is accelerated more when Ca2+ binds syt1 than Doc2α.
source: We assumed that the fusion rate is accelerated more when Ca2+ binds syt1 than Doc2α.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model structure.

claim: In the model, syt7 acts as a catalyst for docking, increasing both docking and undocking rates.
source: Like Doc2α and syt1, which reduce the energy barrier for exocytosis upon Ca2+ binding, we assumed that syt7 acts as a catalyst for docking (Walter et al., 2013). Because docking, unlike fusion, is reversible (Kusick et al., 2020; Murthy and Stevens, 1999; Yavuz et al., 2018), a reduction in the barrier height alone (without a change in the free energies of the docked or undocked states) increases both the docking and the undocking rates.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model structure, supported by citations.

claim: The catalytic function of syt7 in the model is consistent with observations that its loss did not affect steady-state docking.
source: Such a catalytic function of syt7 is consistent with the observations that (1) its loss did not affect steady-state docking (Figure 6) and that (2) during transient docking in cultured hippocampal neurons, the number of docked vesicles returns to the pre-stimulation baseline.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the model structure to experimental observations.

claim: In the model, Doc2α and syt7 are assumed to be present on the plasma membrane and bind Ca2+ irrespective of whether the site is occupied by a vesicle.
source: Since both Doc2α and syt7 are present on the plasma membrane (Sugita et al., 2001; Verhage et al., 1997; Vevea et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2014), they were assumed to bind Ca2+ irrespective of whether the site is occupied by a vesicle (see 'Methods').
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical model structure, supported by citations about protein localization.

claim: Model simulations indicate that all three sensors (syt1, Doc2α, syt7) reach maximum Ca2+ activation at a similar time.
source: Our simulations indicate that all three sensors reach maximum Ca2+ activation at a similar time (Figure 7C), despite slower Ca2+-binding rates of syt7 and Doc2α compared to syt1.
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7C.

claim: In model simulations, syt1's low Ca2+ affinity but fast binding kinetics ensure that its Ca2+ association closely follows the shape of the Ca2+ transient.
source: However, syt1's low Ca2+ affinity but fast binding kinetics ensure that its Ca2+ association closely follows the shape of the Ca2+ transient itself (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7C.

claim: In model simulations, the activation of syt1 by Ca2+ dominated the synchronous release observed immediately after the first action potential.
source: The activation of syt1 by Ca2+ dominated the synchronous release observed immediately after the first AP as removal of syt7 and Doc2α from the model did not affect the peak release rate (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7G.

claim: In model simulations, asynchronous release in response to a single action potential strongly depended on the delayed and sustained activation of Doc2α.
source: By contrast, AR in response to a single AP strongly depended on the delayed and sustained activation of Doc2α (Figure 7C F).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7C and F.

claim: In model simulations, syt7 did not contribute noticeably to neurotransmitter release induced by the first action potential due to its assigned role in docking.
source: Although Doc2α and syt7 have the same Ca2+-binding dynamics in the model, syt7 did not contribute noticeably to neurotransmitter release induced by the first AP (Figure 7F and G) due to its assigned role in docking.
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7F and G.

claim: In model simulations during train stimulation, synchronous release gradually decreased while asynchronous release showed the opposite trend.
source: During the stimulus train in simulations of the control condition, synchronous release gradually decreased, while AR showed the opposite trend (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7F and G.

claim: In model simulations, removal of Doc2α caused reduced depression of synchronous release and reduced asynchronous release.
source: Removal of Doc2α from the model caused a reduced depression of synchronous release and reduced AR (compare Figure 7E and G with Figures 3D and 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7E and G, compared to experimental data.

claim: In model simulations, Ca2+-bound syt7 ensured fast recovery of docked vesicles after depletion.
source: Ca2+-bound syt7 ensured a fast recovery of docked vesicles after depletion (independent of whether fusion depended on Doc2α and Syt1 or Syt1 alone, Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7D.

claim: In model simulations, removal of syt7 resulted in very limited recovery of docked vesicles before the next stimulus.
source: As observed experimentally in the syt7 KO (Figure 6), removal of this catalytic function in the model resulted in very limited recovery of docked vesicles before the next stimulus (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7D, compared to experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: In model simulations, removal of syt7 resulted in reduction of both synchronous and asynchronous release modes.
source: Because under prolonged stimulation both synchronous and asynchronous release depend on vesicle replenishment, removal of syt7 from the model resulted in the reduction of both release modes (Figure 7E and G).
evidence: This is a finding from mathematical modeling presented in Figure 7E and G.

claim: There is good qualitative correspondence between the model and experimental data.
source: Thus, there is a good qualitative correspondence of our models to the experimental data.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of modeling results to experimental data.

claim: The results of experiments are consistent with a sequential role of syt7 and Doc2α in promoting synaptic vesicle docking and fusion, respectively.
source: This demonstrates that the results of our experiments are consistent with a sequential role of syt7 and Doc2α in promoting synaptic vesicle docking and fusion, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of modeling results to experimental data.

claim: Loss of both Doc2α and syt7 was not additive with respect to asynchronous release after single action potentials.
source: We first applied single action potentials and observed that loss of both proteins was not additive with respect to AR: the reduction in slow EPSC charge was identical in Doc2α neurons compared to Doc2α/syt7 DKOs (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from epistasis experiments using double knockout mice presented in Figure 8A and B.

claim: No differences in asynchronous release were observed between Doc2α KO and Doc2α/syt7 DKO during train stimulation.
source: Importantly, no differences in AR were observed between the Doc2α KO and the Doc2α/syt7 DKO condition.
evidence: This is a finding from epistasis experiments using double knockout mice during train stimulation.

claim: The DKO showed different short-term plasticity phenotype than either single KO.
source: However, the DKO showed a different short-term plasticity phenotype than either single KO.
evidence: This is a finding from epistasis experiments using double knockout mice.

claim: Synchronous release early in the train was similar in DKOs to EGTA-treated neurons, with abolished paired-pulse facilitation.
source: Synchronous release early in the train was similar in DKOs to EGTA-treated neurons, with abolished paired-pulse facilitation but not the enhanced depression seen in syt7 KOs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from epistasis experiments using double knockout mice presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the DKO, late in the train amplitudes decayed to the same lower level as syt7 KOs.
source: However, in the DKO, late in the train amplitudes decayed to the same lower level as syt7 KOs, suggesting a specific role for syt7 in limiting steady-state depression.
evidence: This is a finding from epistasis experiments using double knockout mice.

claim: The epistasis experiment findings strongly support a sequential model for the action of syt7 and Doc2α.
source: Together, these findings strongly support a sequential model for the action of syt7 and Doc2α (illustrated in Figure 9, as detailed below).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from epistasis experiments.

claim: Synaptic vesicles rapidly transition from undocked to docked states during activity.
source: Recent studies have proposed that synaptic vesicles rapidly transition from undocked to docked states during activity, and that this could, in principle, provide a common basis for AR, synaptic facilitation, and resistance to synaptic depression (Chang et al., 2018; Kobbersmed et al., 2020; Kusick et al., 2022; Miki et al., 2018; Miki et al., 2016; Neher and Brose, 2018; Silva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of recent literature proposing a mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: A substantial fraction of vesicles undock in response to an action potential and enter into a dynamic state in which they re-dock within 15 ms.
source: Consistent with this notion, we previously found that a substantial fraction of vesicles undock in response to an action potential, and enter into a dynamic state in which they re-dock, within 15 ms, to replenish vacated release sites.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Transient docking was blocked by EGTA-AM.
source: Importantly, like AR and facilitation, transient docking was blocked by EGTA-AM.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Syt7 is strongly enriched at the plasma membrane, not on synaptic vesicles.
source: Curiously, syt7, unlike the fast syts and like the other apparent 'docking sensor' syt3 (Weingarten et al., 2022), is strongly enriched not on synaptic vesicles but at the plasma membrane (Liu et al., 2014; Vevea et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Syt7 is nonfunctional when directed to synaptic vesicles.
source: In fact, it is nonfunctional when directed to synaptic vesicles (Vevea et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Outside the synapse and in non-neuronal cells, syt7 localizes to dense-core vesicles and lysosomes and seems to trigger exocytosis directly.
source: This is in contrast to syt7's actions outside the synapse and in non-neuronal cells, where it localizes to dense-core vesicles and lysosomes and seems to trigger exocytosis directly (Chakrabarti et al., 2003; Tawfik et al., 2021; van Westen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Targeting to the plasma membrane may be relevant to a role in Ca2+-triggered docking as opposed to fusion.
source: These are all hints that targeting to the plasma membrane may be relevant to a role in Ca2+-triggered docking as opposed to fusion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the localization data and functional observations.

claim: The model qualitatively recapitulated the dynamics observed in experimental data.
source: We confirmed that the dynamics observed in the experimental data could be qualitatively recapitulated by a mathematical model in which syt7 and Doc2α act to promote synaptic vesicle docking and fusion, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from mathematical modeling.

claim: Both experiments and modeling showed that syt7-mediated docking promotes synchronous and asynchronous release from the second stimulus onward.
source: Both experiments and modeling showed (1) that syt7-mediated docking promotes synchronous and AR from the second stimulus onward, and (2) that Doc2α promotes AR at the cost of synchronous release.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integration of experimental and modeling data.

claim: Both experiments and modeling showed that Doc2α promotes asynchronous release at the cost of synchronous release.
source: Both experiments and modeling showed (1) that syt7-mediated docking promotes synchronous and AR from the second stimulus onward, and (2) that Doc2α promotes AR at the cost of synchronous release.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integration of experimental and modeling data.

claim: In the model, syt7 acts as a catalyst for synaptic vesicle docking, ensuring that the number of docked vesicles at rest is independent of the presence of syt7.
source: In our model, syt7 acts as a catalyst for synaptic vesicle docking, meaning that Ca2+-bound syt7 enhances both docking and undocking rates. This ensures that the number of docked vesicles at rest is independent of the presence of syt7, accounting for the observation that steady-state docking is normal in syt7 KO neurons (Vevea et al., 2021; this study).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure and its consistency with experimental observations.

claim: If syt7 functions as a docking catalyst, the number of docked vesicles cannot overshoot during repetitive stimulation, but only return to baseline.
source: If syt7 functions as a docking catalyst, the number of docked vesicles cannot overshoot during repetitive stimulation, but only return to baseline.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model structure.

claim: The catalytic function of syt7 does not explain the established role of syt7 in facilitation, as facilitation has been proposed to depend on an increase in the number of docked/primed vesicles.
source: While this is consistent with the EM data presented here, it does not explain the established role of syt7 in facilitation (Jackman et al., 2016) as facilitation has been proposed to depend on an increase in the number of docked/primed vesicles (Jusyte et al., 2023; Kobbersmed et al., 2020; Miki et al., 2016; Neher and Brose, 2018).
evidence: This is a discussion of a limitation of the model, supported by citations.

claim: It remains possible that syt7 selectively alters docking or undocking rates.
source: Therefore, it remains possible that syt7 selectively alters docking or undocking rates.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Another model previously showed that syt3 promotes Ca2+-dependent docking.
source: Corresponding to the role of syt7 in our model, another model previously showed that syt3 promotes Ca2+-dependent docking (Weingarten et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The cultured hippocampal neurons used only facilitate very slightly.
source: At the moment, it is difficult to know since the cultured hippocampal neurons we used only facilitate very slightly (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Synaptic vesicle exocytosis in the model was simulated following the dual-sensor model.
source: Synaptic vesicle exocytosis in the model was simulated following the dual-sensor model (Kobbersmed et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2007), in which Ca2+ binds to two different sensors promoting fusion (Doc2α and syt1 in the model presented here).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure, based on prior modeling approaches.

claim: The model diverged from the dual-sensor model by implementing a competition between syt1 and Doc2α for Ca2+ binding.
source: We diverged from the dual-sensor model by implementing a competition between syt1 and Doc2α for Ca2+ binding.
evidence: This is a description of a modification to the model structure.

claim: Competition between syt1 and Doc2α was needed to recapitulate the reduced depression observed in Doc2α KO neurons compared to WT controls.
source: This competition was needed to recapitulate the reduced depression observed in Doc2αKO neurons compared to WT controls (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a justification for the model structure based on experimental observations.

claim: The direct competition between Doc2α and syt1 could indicate a need to act at a limited number of 'slots' at the release site.
source: The direct competition between Doc2α and syt1 could indicate a need to act at a limited number of 'slots' at the release site (e.g., SNARE complexes or lipid clusters; Chen et al., 2021; Groffen et al., 2010; Honigmann et al., 2013; Kobbersmed et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about the molecular basis of the competition, supported by citations.

claim: The apparent competition between asynchronous and synchronous release over a limited supply of docked vesicles may play a role in the slower depression of synchronous release observed in Doc2α KOs.
source: Additionally, the apparent competition between AR and synchronous release over a limited supply of docked vesicles (as proposed by Otsu et al., 2004 and Yao et al., 2011, and suggested by the EM here) may play a role in the slower depression of synchronous release observed in Doc2α KOs.
evidence: This is a speculation about mechanisms, supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: The model describes the association to 'slots' implicitly by lumping it together with Ca2+ binding and synaptic vesicle fusion.
source: Our model describes the association to 'slots' implicitly by lumping it together with Ca2+ binding and synaptic vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is a description of a simplification in the model structure.

claim: The model can only account for Ca2+-dependent functions of the included proteins.
source: This also means that our model can only account for Ca2+-dependent functions of the included proteins.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the model.

claim: Recent analysis indicates that syt1 pre-associates with slots at resting Ca2+ concentrations, which would limit access to these slots for other sensors.
source: Recent analysis, however, indicates that syt1 pre-associates with these slots at resting Ca2+ concentrations, which would limit access to these slots for other sensors (Kobbersmed et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: Pre-association of syt1 with slots would account for the reported clamping syt1 exerts on spontaneous transmission and asynchronous release.
source: This arrangement would account for the reported clamping syt1 exerts on spontaneous transmission (Courtney et al., 2019; Kochubey and Schneggenburger, 2011; Schupp et al., 2016) and AR (Maximov and Südhof, 2005; Nishiki and Augustine, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference about mechanisms, supported by citations.
